extra_misconceptions.fact: Recorded broadcasts, movies, and television adaptations are prohibited; you must attend live stage performances or read the scripts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Streaming a filmed Broadway broadcast at home satisfies the live viewing option for the three required full-length plays.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Effective reviews summarize the premise briefly while dedicating most analysis to acting choices, directorial pacing, and staging.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A strong theater review focuses almost entirely on retelling every scene of the plot from the opening curtain to the finale.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Acting critique examines vocal projection, physical characterization, emotional truth, and how performers listen and react in scenes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Evaluating stage acting requires judging only whether the performers memorized all their lines without stumbling on stage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Phone screens distract actors and audience members; jot brief notes on a notepad during intermission or right after the curtain falls.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Using a bright smartphone screen during a live performance is the standard way to log detailed notes for your written review.

extra_socratic_questions: Under what condition does a dramatic production qualify as an eligible performance rather than a prohibited recorded screening?
What distinguishes a mere plot summary from an analytical critique of blocking, vocal projection, and scenic transitions?
When should a reviewer record observations about lighting cues and actor pacing so playhouse etiquette stays intact?
Which structural elements in a printed script reveal staging intent when you read a full-length play instead of attending live?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standard playscript formatting averages about one minute per page, so a ten-minute one-act play typically requires ten to twelve pages.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Three pages of single-spaced prose dialogue are enough to fill ten full minutes of live stage performance time.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The climax is the decisive turning point where the protagonist confronts the central conflict, followed by a brief falling resolution.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The climax of a one-act play is simply the final line spoken right before the stage lights fade to black.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stage scripts use theatrical blocking terms like upstage and downstage rather than cinematic camera movements meant for film sets.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Playwrights should write detailed camera angles and close-up instructions into the stage directions of a theater script.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Conflict arises whenever a main character faces a meaningful obstacle blocking an urgent goal, even in quiet conversational scenes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dramatic conflict in a script requires physical combat or loud shouting matches between two opposing characters.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that your draft script will run at least ten minutes on stage when spoken at a natural pace?
What separates the inciting incident that starts the dramatic conflict from the climax where that conflict reaches its peak?
Why must a playwright reveal the protagonist's internal struggle through active dialogue and stage business instead of narration?
What happens to the dramatic momentum of a ten-minute one-act play if the script demands complex set changes between scenes?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every overhead lighting instrument must be wrench-tightened and secured to the pipe with a separate steel safety cable.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tightening a C-clamp bolt by hand is sufficient to keep an overhead stage light from falling onto the performers below.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Backstage shops require closed-toe shoes, tied-back hair, and eye protection whenever crew members build, rig, or paint scenery.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Open-toed sandals and loose clothing are safe to wear during set construction as long as you only paint flats.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fire lanes, exit doors, and extinguisher cabinets must remain completely unobstructed at all times during rehearsals and shows.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Fire exits and backstage crossovers make convenient storage space for large set pieces during a fast scene change.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The acting option requires playing either one major role in a full-length production or roles across three separate one-act plays.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Acting a minor walk-on role in a single ten-minute skit fulfills the acting specialization option for this requirement.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to adjust counterweights on an unbalanced batten without calling a heads-up warning to the stage floor?
Where should a stage crew apply spike tape and phosphorescent glow tape so actors can exit safely during a complete blackout?
Which secondary restraint must attach every overhead lighting fixture to the pipe before the technician steps off the ladder?
What distinguishes a director's artistic blocking decisions during rehearsal from a stage manager's cue calling during a run?

extra_misconceptions.fact: True pantomime communicates story and emotion entirely through posture, gesture, and facial expression without mouthing dialogue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Mouthing silent words to another imaginary character is the best way to explain the plot during a solo pantomime routine.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Your fingers and wrists must maintain fixed spacing and muscular tension until you deliberately set the imaginary object down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hand position can relax and collapse as soon as you finish lifting an invisible object off the floor in a mime scene.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Deliberate movements with crisp clicks at the start and end of each contact define the exact boundaries of unseen objects.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Fast, frantic hand waving makes invisible objects easier for the audience to recognize during a pantomime performance.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Keeping your chin lifted and chest open projects facial expressions to the house so spectators can read the emotional shift.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Looking down at the floor while pantomiming an emotional reaction helps the audience feel a character's disappointment.

extra_socratic_questions: Which physical indicator shows the audience that an imaginary book picked up from a puddle has realistic weight and thickness?
What happens to the illusion of a furnished room if a mime walks straight through the spot where a table was just touched?
In what order should your eyes, face, and hands react when you spot the departing bus so the audience reads the moment clearly?
Why must a performer inspect the floor surface and warm up joints before executing a slip or crouch near an imaginary puddle?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stage right and stage left are always defined from the perspective of an actor standing on stage facing the audience.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stage right refers to the right-hand side of the stage as viewed by the audience sitting out in the auditorium seats.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Floodlights lack lenses and cast a wide, unfocused wash over backdrops or cycloramas, whereas spotlights focus tight beams.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A floodlight uses a focusing lens and adjustable shutters to project a sharp, narrow beam onto a single moving actor.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Historical raked stages sloped down toward the audience, so downstage is closest to the viewers and upstage is farthest away.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Downstage is located near the back wall of the stagehouse because historical stages sloped downward away from the house.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Arena staging seats audience members on all four sides, so tall scenery blocks sightlines and must be replaced by low furniture.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tall painted flats can be placed across the middle of an arena stage just like they are used behind a proscenium arch.

extra_socratic_questions: Whose perspective determines stage right and stage left, and why does that convention prevent confusion during blocking calls?
What happens to scenic height limits and actor blocking when a production moves from a proscenium arch to central arena staging?
What measurement on a scaled ground plan confirms that extreme side-seat sightlines will not expose the backstage wing areas?
Under what condition should a crew secure a tall flat with an adjustable stage brace and stage weight rather than flying it?
